# Features

> Run coding agents in parallel, keep terminal sessions running, review diffs, edit files, and coordinate panes with Git worktrees, MCP, and the Paneflow CLI.

Canonical: https://paneflow.dev/docs/features

<!-- Auto-generated mirror of paneflow.dev - do not edit by hand.
     Source of truth: the paneflow.dev docs. Regenerated by
     scripts/sync-public-docs.ts in the site repo. -->

Paneflow is a native terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Run agents side
by side, return to their sessions, and review or edit their changes in the
same window. It runs locally on Linux, macOS, and Windows and is free and
open source under GPL-3.0-or-later.

For your first installation, follow the [getting started guide](/docs).

## Organize projects and panes

Open a project as a **workspace** and organize its tasks in **tabs**. Each
tab contains **panes** where you can run agents, shells, or commands.
Several agents can share a tab and the same checkout. Create a separate
Git worktree when a task needs its own files and branch.

Split the focused pane horizontally with `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+D` or vertically
with `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E`. Each new pane starts a shell in the same working
directory. Move between panes with `Alt+Arrow` and open another workspace
with `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+N`. Use `Cmd` on macOS and `Ctrl` on Linux and Windows.

Use the four [layout presets](/docs/layouts) to arrange panes. Consult
[shortcuts and actions](/docs/keybindings) for keyboard navigation and
custom bindings.

## Run and follow coding agents

Launch Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Pi, Hermes, or another CLI agent
installed on your machine. Each agent runs in an ordinary terminal and
connects to its own model provider. Read its output, interrupt it, or take
over with the keyboard. Open project sessions for coding tasks, or an agent
chat from your home directory (`~`) for research and planning outside a project.

Claude Code and Codex can report whether they are working, waiting for input,
finished, or in an error state through lifecycle hooks. Install these once
per machine with `paneflow integrations install claude-code` or
`paneflow integrations install codex`. Codex asks you to trust the hooks
through `/hooks`. You can also use **Install hooks** in the
[agent settings](/docs/settings). The same command registers the Paneflow
MCP bridge and, for Claude Code, the conductor skill. An entry that another
Paneflow home owns (a debug build next to a release, or a second
`PANEFLOW_HOME`) is left alone: the command names both homes, and `--force`
takes the entry over.

For agents without hooks, Paneflow estimates activity from the running
processes and terminal output. Status tracking depends on the agent integration.
Use `paneflow sessions` to read session status even when the window is closed.
The [automation guide](/docs/scripting) explains hooks and events.

On Linux and macOS, the **Claude Code (team)** launcher entry starts Claude
Code with agent teams enabled and opens each teammate in its own Paneflow
pane, next to the lead's pane, instead of inside the lead's terminal. Claude
Code drives those panes through `tmux` commands, which Paneflow answers
itself for that pane only: every other pane keeps your real `tmux` and
`PATH`. A team can only open, list, rename, and close its own panes. Typing
into a teammate with `send-keys` follows the same `PANEFLOW_IPC_SCRIPTING`
rule as `paneflow send`. Closing the lead's pane leaves the teammates open
as ordinary panes. The entry does not exist on Windows: Claude Code's
terminal team mode needs tmux and a POSIX shell there, so on Windows
teammates run inside the lead's pane.

## Keep terminal sessions running

When quitting Paneflow, choose **Keep sessions running** to leave shells
and agents running. Reopen the app to reconnect to those sessions and their
terminal screens. Choose **Stop everything and quit** to end the processes.

Sessions run in a separate local host process. They stay alive while that
host and your machine remain running. A machine restart or host crash ends
the processes. Paneflow also saves the layout and working directories.

When a pane's session did not survive a reboot, a host stop, or a lost host,
Paneflow restores the conversation the agent was running: it opens a shell in
the recorded folder and types the agent's resume command, such as
`claude --resume <id>` for Claude Code, `codex resume <id>` for Codex (with
`-c check_for_update_on_startup=false` added), or `fx --continue` for fx.
Paneflow records the conversation from the agent's SessionStart hook and
forgets it when the agent ends or the pane returns to its shell prompt. If the
folder is gone, the shell opens in your home folder under a
`Folder not found: <path>` banner. If the resume fails within 15 seconds, a
`Resume failed: <reason>` banner offers **New session**. A conversation
restored in several panes resumes only in the first. To only reopen the shell,
set `"agents": {"restore_conversations": false}`; see the
[`agents` settings](/docs/configuration/schema#agents).

**Fork conversation**, in the pane context menu and the command palette, opens
a branch of a Claude Code or Codex conversation in a split to the right.

When closing a pane, tab, or workspace brings up a confirmation, choose
**Keep running** to preserve its sessions or **Stop** to end their processes.
To remove a pane from the layout while keeping its process alive, choose
**Hide from layout (keeps running)** in the pane menu. Reopen the session
from the sidebar.

When a shell or command ends, its pane stays open with the final output in
read-only mode. Choose **Restart** to open a new shell. To resume an agent
conversation, use that agent's own session commands; restarting the shell
does not resume the conversation.

Use **Undo** after closing a tab, or `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+T` to reopen the most
recently closed tab or pane. Paneflow reconnects to a retained session when
available; otherwise, it opens a new shell.

## Review and edit changes

Open **Changes** in the dock beside the active tab to compare the checkout
with `HEAD`. It includes staged and unstaged changes and untracked files.
Read split or unified diffs, highlight changes within lines, and revert
individual blocks in modified files. You can also trim or ignore whitespace.

Open **Files** to browse the file tree and edit code in the integrated
editor. Save changes, undo, or redo. Git markers beside the lines open a
popup to read, copy, or revert the previous text. If a file changes on disk
while you edit it, Paneflow lets you resolve the save conflict.

See examples in the [diff viewer guide](/blog/diff-viewer) and the
[file tree and editor guide](/blog/files-sidebar).

## Keep project context at hand

The branch display and file tree follow the active checkout. Copy absolute
or relative file paths for prompts and commands. Use `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+I` in
a terminal to find a file by name and insert its path, quoted for the shell.

Paste an image to save it under `~/.paneflow/cache/clipboard-images/` and
insert its path. Claude Code and Codex can attach that path as an image.

Paneflow associates listening ports with the panes running their processes.
Recognized development servers can show clickable URLs. Pin frequent build,
test, lint, or server commands as custom buttons using
[shortcuts and actions](/docs/keybindings).

## Separate tasks with Git worktrees

Use a Git worktree when parallel tasks need separate checkouts. Each can
have its own branch, files, panes, and agent sessions while sharing Git
history. Worktrees are optional: agents can also work in the same checkout.

Separate checkouts do not prevent merge conflicts or isolate running
programs. The [worktree guide](/docs/worktrees) covers creation, reuse,
cleanup, and snapshots of uncommitted files before removal.

## Share pane output through MCP

Install the local MCP bridge with `paneflow mcp install` for Claude Code,
Codex, Gemini CLI, or OpenCode. Its `list_panes`, `read_pane`, and
`search_pane` tools let an agent read another pane's output without you
copying terminal history between conversations.

Output is returned as untrusted data for the reading agent to analyze.
Its one write tool, `write_pane`, sends a message to another agent's pane
only after you allow that pair of agent sessions in Paneflow. The bridge
cannot send keystrokes or control panes in any other way. See
[MCP setup and behavior](/docs/scripting).

## Coordinate panes with the CLI

Use the local `paneflow` CLI to list agents, read output, wait for a result,
or follow activity events. Scripts and agents can also create or control
panes when the relevant permissions are enabled.

- `paneflow up` opens a workspace from a file defining its panes,
  working directories, commands, and prompts.
- `paneflow flow run` executes steps defined in `flow.toml`, waits for
  dependencies or output patterns, and captures results.

`paneflow send` prefills text. Add `--submit` to press Enter explicitly.
Writing and submission require the corresponding permissions; launching
panes with commands or prompts also requires an orchestration or scripting
permission. The [CLI automation guide](/docs/scripting) explains these controls.

For a workflow that reads agent progress, sends a prompt, and waits for a
report, follow the [Conductor guide](/docs/conductor).

## Adjust Paneflow to your workflow

Use [Settings](/docs/settings) to choose the shell, theme, terminal display,
shortcuts, notifications, workspace templates, and agent access controls.
Many changes apply while the app is running; a new default shell applies
to new terminals.

For file-based configuration and advanced options, use the
[`paneflow.json` reference](/docs/configuration). For installation, graphics,
shell, or font problems, follow the [troubleshooting guide](/docs/troubleshooting).
